clue.text: War-time craft of a bloodsucker?

definitions.meaning: the de Havilland ... was a famous fast wooden aircraft of the Second World War
a biting insect that feeds on blood

explanation.surface: A question about which wartime vessel belonged to some blood-drinking creature.
explanation.definitionFit: One name serves both a Second World War aeroplane and the familiar biting insect.

clue.text: A nice do, involving a sea nymph

indicators.note: the letters are wound together and turned about, giving a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A pleasant party that includes a mermaid-like guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' here means twisting up, so A NICE DO is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the daughters of the Titan Oceanus were nymphs of the ocean.

clue.text: Measure associated with lobsters

definitions.meaning: an old word for a stately dance
the Mock Turtle and Gryphon dance the Lobster ... in Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: A unit of size connected with shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: A square dance for four couples, the kind Lewis Carroll's creatures perform with lobsters.

clue.text: These clubs are for swingers

parts.note: bottle-shaped wooden clubs swung in gymnastic exercise

explanation.surface: Some nightclubs catering for the free-living set.
explanation.walkthrough: Indian clubs are bowling-pin-shaped weights swung round the body in old-fashioned exercise drills.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the exercise clubs swung by gymnasts comes from the subcontinent where they originated.

clue.text: Pupils' examiner

parts.note: not a school inspector but a specialist who looks into the eye's pupils

explanation.surface: Someone who sets tests for schoolchildren.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye specialist doctor examines the pupils of patients' eyes.

clue.text: Old gown locally associated with Virgil

definitions.meaning: a loose robe worn by women in the 17th and 18th centuries
the Italian city near which the poet Virgil was born

explanation.surface: Some antique garment said to have ties with the Roman poet's home region.
explanation.definitionFit: The historical gown took its name from the Italian city that was the poet's birthplace.

clue.text: State of Selkirk the surveyor ?

parts.note: Cowper's poem on the castaway Alexander Selkirk begins 'I am monarch of all I survey'

explanation.surface: A question about where a land surveyor named Selkirk comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Selkirk, the real Robinson Crusoe, is the speaker of Cowper's lines 'I am monarch of all I survey'; his island realm is a one-man kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm ruled by a sovereign, as Selkirk ruled all he surveyed.

clue.text: Pitman devised one of these drums

indicators.note: the name's letters are worked into a newly invented order

parts.note: the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Isaac Pitman, the shorthand inventor, created a type of drum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devised' rearranges PITMAN into TIMPAN; Pitman invented a shorthand system, which makes 'devised' look natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Kettledrums of the orchestra are known by this Italian plural.

clue.text: Made marginal contributions to literary work

definitions.text: Made marginal contributions to literary work

parts.words: Made marginal contributions to literary work
parts.note: wrote comments in the margins of a text

explanation.surface: Contributed only slightly to a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marginal' suggests minor, but it means literally in the margins.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplying a text with explanatory notes in its margins.

clue.text: One's own war engine may hoist one

definitions.text: One's own war engine may hoist one

parts.words: One's own war engine may hoist one
parts.note: plays on the saying about being hoist with your own explosive device, a schemer undone by his own trap

explanation.surface: A siege weapon that ends up lifting the person who built it.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Hamlet gives the phrase 'hoist with his own petard', blown up by one's own bomb; the clue simply describes that small explosive device.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bomb used to breach gates in old sieges, remembered from the idiom about self-inflicted ruin.

clue.text: Tough chap outside northern church, a good supporter

indicators.note: the tough chap's letters sit around the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: a he-man is a strong, macho fellow

explanation.surface: A burly man standing outside a church in the north, described as a loyal backer.
explanation.definitionFit: A faithful follower or right-hand man, the kind of loyal aide who backs a leader.

clue.text: Intrude, or chance replacement

indicators.note: the letters are put back in a new order, rearranged into a different word

explanation.surface: Someone choosing between forcing their way in or leaving it to luck as a substitute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacement' signals that the eight letters of OR and CHANCE are placed afresh in another order.
explanation.definitionFit: To trespass or advance gradually onto another's territory or rights is to intrude.

clue.text: Dad tucked into the rest of the meal

indicators.note: one word is placed snugly inside the other, as a child is tucked into bed

parts.note: taken as written
Pa is a familiar word for father

explanation.surface: Father helping himself to whatever is left of dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'tucked into' as eating heartily, but here it marks one word placed inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal word for a meal or a spread of food.

clue.text: Some young lad, ultimately

indicators.note: only part of the following words is taken, a run of letters lying across them

explanation.surface: A boy who will, in the end, grow up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' signals letters taken from inside 'young lAD ULTimately'; the whole clue also describes the answer, since a lad eventually becomes grown-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy, given time, becomes a grown-up person.

clue.text: Girl put on weight? Right, he tells us

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
an ounce is a small unit of weight

explanation.surface: A young woman has gained weight, and someone confirms it.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcaster or herald who informs the public of news.

clue.text: Subtle Jonsonian with the Midas touch?

definitions.text: Subtle Jonsonian with the Midas touch?

parts.words: Subtle Jonsonian with the Midas touch
parts.note: Subtle is the trickster in Ben Jonson's comedy who claims he can turn base metal into gold, like King Midas

explanation.surface: A clever character from Ben Jonson's plays who seems able to make gold.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's 1610 comedy is named after its swindler Subtle, who pretends to transmute metals; 'Subtle' looks like an adjective but is his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A practitioner of the medieval art that sought to turn lead into gold, as Midas turned everything.

clue.text: 4 princess

parts.note: the solution to 4 down, a word meaning from the subcontinent, placed before princess

explanation.surface: Bare cross-reference: a royal lady of the land named at 4.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 4 as INDIAN: an Indian princess, or the wife of a maharaja.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu queen or princess, the wife of a great prince of the subcontinent.

clue.text: Nokomis in relation to the moon

definitions.text: Nokomis in relation to the moon

parts.words: Nokomis in relation to the moon
parts.note: in Longfellow's Hiawatha, Nokomis, the hero's grandmother, fell from the moon as its child

explanation.surface: A question about how the grandmother in Hiawatha is related to the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's poem calls Nokomis 'Daughter of the Moon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nokomis is the moon's female child in Longfellow's poem.

clue.text: A fractionally higher figure?.

parts.note: in a written fraction, the number placed above the line

explanation.surface: A number that is only slightly bigger than another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fractionally higher' seems to mean 'a little larger', but it means 'higher up in a fraction': the top number.
explanation.definitionFit: In a fraction such as three quarters, the number on top is the one being divided.

clue.text: Colour of publication in French volunteer force?

parts.note: mag is short for magazine
en is French for in
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: Asking what shade a magazine uses for a French volunteer regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA, the Territorial Army, is the British Army's part-time volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: A vivid purplish red dye, named after an Italian battle.

clue.text: Less than half get a degree in criminology

definitions.meaning: one part of three, smaller than a half
the ... degree is harsh police interrogation

explanation.surface: Getting a poor university grade in the study of crime.
explanation.walkthrough: A British third-class honours degree is the lowest grade; the second sense is 'the third degree', tough questioning of a suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: One of three equal parts is smaller than a half, and the harsh grilling of suspects is called the third degree.

clue.text: Tell a story about Robert of Paris, for one

parts.note: re means concerning
Count Robert of Paris is the title character of a Walter Scott novel, so he is an example of a nobleman

explanation.surface: Narrating a tale concerning Robert of Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for one' marks Robert as an example of a count, from Scott's novel Count Robert of Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate or relate events in order.

clue.text: I thus block a cartographer's line

parts.note: so means in this way
to bar is to obstruct

explanation.surface: Someone stopping a mapmaker from drawing a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A line on a weather map joining points of equal atmospheric pressure.

clue.text: Advocating Chaldean drink? Grand:

parts.note: Ur was a city of the Chaldees in ancient Mesopotamia
gin is a spirit
G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: Pressing the merits of some ancient Babylonian liquor and calling it splendid.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing a case or pushing a course of action is advocating it.

clue.text: Block was, let once

definitions.meaning: to stand in the way of something
in old usage, to let was to hinder, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A building that was formerly rented out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let' looks like renting, but its archaic sense is to hinder, surviving in tennis and in the phrase 'without let or hindrance'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hinder or impede, the archaic sense of the verb let, is to stand in the way.

clue.text: Matrimonial papers?

parts.note: not marriage documents but the scraps of coloured paper thrown over a bride and groom

explanation.surface: Official documents for a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Small pieces of coloured paper showered on newly-weds after a wedding.

clue.text: Ford's Latin history?

parts.note: Henry Ford said history is bunk; give that word a Latin-looking ending

explanation.surface: A book on ancient Rome by someone called Ford.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Ford, the American carmaker, famously said 'History is bunk'; adding the Latin-style -UM gives a word for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Ford dismissed history as nonsense, and the longer form of his word means empty claptrap.

clue.text: He's paid for his work per ear perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the preceding words are only one possible arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: A farm labourer whose wages are counted by each ear of corn harvested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells us to rearrange PER EAR; the surface fits, since a harvest hand might be paid by the ear of corn.
explanation.definitionFit: A harvester who cuts crops is a hired labourer paid for the job.

clue.text: Peak charges which fall in a rush

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill top, especially on Dartmoor
rents are payments charged for property

explanation.surface: Mountain fees that drop suddenly.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a craggy hill, common in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Rushing floods of water, or heavy downpours, pour down violently.
